question: A 68-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of difficulty starting urination, weak stream, and terminal dribbling. The patient has no history of serious illnesses and is not under any medications currently. The patient’s father had prostate cancer at the age of 58 years. Vital signs are within normal range. Upon examination, the urinary bladder is not palpable. Further examination reveals normal anal sphincter tone and a bulbocavernosus muscle reflex. Digital rectal exam (DRE) shows a prostate size equivalent to 2 finger pads with a hard nodule and without fluctuance or tenderness. The prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 5 ng/mL. Image-guided biopsy indicates prostate cancer. MRI shows tumor confined within the prostate. Radionuclide bone scan reveals no abnormalities. Which of the following interventions is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Difficulty starting urination, weak stream, terminal dribbling" -> "Suspicion of prostate issue" -> "Family history of prostate cancer" -> "PSA level of 5 ng/mL" -> "Prostate cancer diagnosis confirmed by biopsy" -> "Tumor confined within the prostate on MRI" -> "No bone metastasis on radionuclide bone scan" -> 95%
enhanced_information: The patient with localized prostate cancer and no bone metastasis should undergo radical prostatectomy + radiation therapy as the most appropriate next step in management.
analysis: The core medical principle in the management of localized prostate cancer without bone metastasis is to consider radical treatment options to achieve the best chance of cure. Radical prostatectomy combined with radiation therapy is a standard approach for localized disease. This combination aims to remove the prostate gland surgically and deliver targeted radiation to the area, maximizing the chances of eradicating the cancer. Chemotherapy is not typically the first-line treatment for localized prostate cancer. Androgen deprivation therapy alone is not sufficient for localized disease without metastasis. Finasteride and tamsulosin are not appropriate for the management of prostate cancer. Radical prostatectomy combined with radiation therapy aligns with the enhanced information provided.
